issues.issue: Section 5.5's saving of each state's power to "enforce any additional conditions and restrictions" against pollution is hard to square with Section 5.2, under which the commission "may assume jurisdiction" to control pollution, and with Section 10.8's supersession rule. Whether a stricter state rule survives commission occupation of the field is the point of tension.

The commission may adopt only "recommended standards" for flood plain land use, yet Section 6.3 requires its own flood land acquisitions to be "in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2." Whether standards that are merely recommended can have binding effect is left unresolved.

Paragraph (b) allows the commission to "establish encroachment lines" and standards for flood plain use, which reads as regulatory, while paragraph (a) confines its power to "recommended standards" that cannot restrict state or local zoning. The two paragraphs describe different legal effects for the same standards.

Section 6.3 requires acquisitions to be "in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2," but Section 6.2(a) authorizes only "recommended standards" that expressly do not restrict local land use power. The condition on the acquisition power thus points to a source that may have no binding content.

The commission may not operate a project unless it finds "no other suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions" — neither "suitable" nor "reasonable conditions" is given content. The bar to the commission's own operation is therefore unmeasurable.

Section 8.1 directs that the commission "shall provide for the development" of recreational facilities and may construct and administer them, but makes this "subject to ... Section 8.2," which forbids it to operate any such facility where another government unit is available. The mandatory duty and the operating bar have to be reconciled.

The operating bar turns on whether another "suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions," terms that are undefined and left to the commission's own finding. No benchmark of suitability or reasonableness is supplied anywhere in Article 8.

The duties are imposed "within limits prescribed by this article," but Article 8 prescribes no express limits other than the Section 8.2(b) operating bar and the Section 8.4 bidding requirement. What the phrase restricts is indeterminate.

Section 8.4 mandates competitive sealed bidding for all private concessions, but Section 15.1(l) provides that Section 8.4 "shall not be construed to apply to facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law." Which concessions escape the bidding requirement depends on reading the two together.

"The business of direct sale to consumers" is not defined, and the same sentence authorizes transmission facilities "for the purpose of wholesale marketing of power." The line between prohibited direct sale and permitted wholesale marketing is unmarked.

Development contracts must be on "reasonable terms, consideration and duration," a standard with no benchmark and no cross-reference to the rate standards of Section 9.5. Reasonableness of consideration in particular has no stated measure.

Power rates must be "reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and just," but Section 3.7 lets the commission fix rates "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party." Who tests the rates against that standard, and by what measure, is not stated.

Section 10.1 lets the commission delegate its regulatory powers to signatory parties, while New York's § 637 forbids any of its agencies to accept a delegation it could not exercise on its own account absent the compact. The delegation power and the state enactment do not sit comfortably together.

A protected area may be declared where demands "have developed or threaten to develop to such a degree as to create a water shortage," with no definition of shortage or of the degree of threat required. "Threaten to develop" gives the designation power no measurable trigger.

The permit requirement excepts withdrawals "pursuant to a permit or approval heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states," but Section 10.8 provides that state-issued diversion and withdrawal permits are superseded to the extent of any conflict with commission regulation. The grandfather clause and the supersession clause cannot both be given full effect.

The emergency provision bars any entity from withdrawing water "for any purpose" in excess of prescribed quantities, without the grandfather exception that Section 10.3 gives to pre-existing state permits and without regard to Sections 3.3(a) and 3.5's protection of decree diversions. Whether decree and pre-existing rights survive an emergency declaration is unaddressed.

Permits turn on avoiding depletion that "will adversely affect the comprehensive plan or the just and equitable interests and rights of other lawful users," while "giving due regard to the need to balance and reconcile alternative and conflicting uses." The standard names competing considerations without any rule of priority among them.

Judicial review is expressly given for determinations under Section 10.2 and permits under Sections 10.3 through 10.5, and for nothing else in Article 10 — inviting an expressio unius argument that actions under Sections 10.7 and 10.8 are unreviewable. The enumeration's exclusivity is the contestable point.

Section 10.8 supersedes state-issued diversion and withdrawal permits "to the extent of any conflict," while Section 10.3(ii) preserves withdrawals made under permits "heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states." The two provisions give opposite answers on pre-existing state permits.

The consultation duty attaches to "all projects related to powers delegated to the commission by this compact," a class defined by an undefined relation to a broad set of delegated powers. What relation suffices is not stated.

Paragraph (b) forbids any federal expenditure or commitment for a project not first included in the comprehensive plan and says it shall not "be deemed authorized," which cannot be squared with paragraph (c)'s preservation of each federal agency's existing authority or with Section 15.1(s)(1)'s preservation of federal powers. The scope of the bar is only intelligible once those provisions are read against it.

Paragraph (c) preserves each federal agency's authority to plan, construct and operate projects "except as specifically provided by this section," while paragraph (b) bars any expenditure on a project not in the comprehensive plan. Whether (b) is such a specific provision, swallowing (c), is the question.

The consultation duty covers "all projects related to powers delegated to the commission by this compact," with no test of relatedness and with "project" carrying the contested Section 1.2(g) definition. Which state and local undertakings are caught is therefore indeterminate.

Paragraph (b) bars any state or local expenditure on a project not first included in the comprehensive plan, while paragraph (c) preserves each state and local agency's existing authority to construct and operate projects. The two paragraphs of the same section pull in opposite directions.

Paragraph (c) preserves state and local agency authority "except as specifically provided by this section," but paragraph (b) forbids the expenditures by which that authority would be exercised. Which is the rule and which the exception cannot be told from the section alone.

The states' reserved right to levy fees and taxes "measured by the withdrawal or diversion of waters" sits against Section 3.5(b), which forbids any fee or charge on decree-permitted diversions, and Section 3.7, which lets the commission fix charges free of state control. Whose exaction survives on the same withdrawal is not settled.

The commission must develop "equitable cost sharing and reimbursement formulas," with equity as the only criterion and no method of determination supplied. The enumerated subparagraphs describe machinery, not the standard.

Section 11.5 has each signatory party "pledge itself to provide technical and administrative services to the commission upon request," but Section 15.1(h) provides that, notwithstanding Section 11.5, federal agencies are pledged only so far as they agree or the President directs. The pledge and the reservation state contradictory obligations for the United States.

The section says bonds "shall be payable solely out of the properties and revenues of the commission without recourse to taxation" and in the next sentence that they "shall be direct and general obligations of the commission" backed by its full faith and credit. The limited-recourse and general-obligation characterizations are in tension.

The sentence reads "The purpose of this compact shall include without limitation thereto all costs of any project or facility," which conflates the compact's purposes with the purposes for which bonds may be issued and borrowed money spent. As written it appears to enlarge Section 1.3's purposes rather than define permitted bond expenditures.

Section 12.3 denies the commission any power to pledge a signatory party's credit or impose bond payment obligations on it, while Section 12.20(b) contemplates bonds sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party." Whether a signatory guaranty is permissible turns on reconciling the two.

The indenture may contain any covenants "other than any restriction on the regulatory powers vested in the commission by this compact," yet the enumerated permissible covenants include covenants as to "the rates or amounts of fees, rents and other charges," which Section 3.7 makes a regulatory power. The exclusion and the enumeration overlap.

"No bond or its terms shall mature in more than fifty years from its own date" is ungrammatical — terms do not mature — and it is unclear whether the fifty-year cap limits final maturity only or every payment obligation under the bond.

Section 12.8 exempts commission bonds and their interest from "all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties," but Section 15.1(f) preserves federal internal revenue taxation of those same bonds except to the extent state bonds are exempt. Since the United States is a signatory party, the two provisions conflict on their face.

Section 12.9 lets the commission set the interest rate without limit, while Section 12.13 caps the net interest cost of a below-par issue at six percent per annum. Whether the 1984 amendment to 12.9 displaced that cap is a question the two sections raise together.

Section 12.13 requires that "all bonds issued and sold for cash pursuant to this act shall be sold on sealed proposals to the highest bidder," while Section 12.20(b) permits delivery to a signatory agency "without public offering" notwithstanding any other provision. The mandatory bidding rule and the exemption must be reconciled.

A validation judgment is declared "conclusive against all persons whomsoever and against each of the signatory parties," without any provision for notice or participation by those bound. Whether the in rem proceeding can bind absent parties as stated is contestable on the face of the words.

The revenues are made a "first, direct and exclusive charge and lien" for bondholders, and in the same sentence may be applied to administration, operation, maintenance, improvements, extensions "or other purposes" as the indenture provides. The exclusivity of the lien and the open-ended exception cannot both be taken at face value.

The signatory parties "will provide such capital funds required for projects," yet the same sentence says nothing in the section "shall be deemed to impose any mandatory obligation on any of the signatory parties." The promise and the disclaimer sit in a single sentence and cancel each other.

Paragraph (b) permits bonds to be sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party," while Section 12.3 denies the commission power to impose any obligation for payment of the bonds upon a signatory party. Whether a guaranty may be given, and by whom, requires reading the two together.
